_note: Plain-language explainers for the ten organs of the Anatomy of AI hero. Prose carries no figures: every number shown in the card is computed at view time from the series files (site/data/series/<id>.json), from policy.json or talent.json, and is cited to that file and its sources. Landmarks are event ids from anatomy_map.json. No em dashes.

compute.label: Compute
compute.desc: Power, chips, training and inference: the physical pipeline that turns electricity into model outputs.

money.label: Money
money.desc: Funding into labs, capital spending on chips, and revenue flowing back from products.

data.label: Data
data.desc: Text, images and code gathered for training, and the usage data that comes back from people.

rules.label: Rules
rules.desc: Laws, export controls and court rulings that constrain labs, chips and data.

people.label: People
people.desc: Researchers and engineers moving into labs, and products reaching the public.

energy>chips.note: Fabs and data centers draw grid power; new sites are planned around where power can be contracted.

energy>labs.note: Training clusters run for weeks at a time, so labs sign long power contracts, including nuclear restarts.

chips>labs.note: Accelerators, sold mostly to clouds and labs, are the scarce input that sets the size of a training run.

capital>labs.note: Venture rounds, strategic investments and cloud credits pay for compute and salaries.

capital>chips.note: Capital spending by clouds and labs lands as chip and data center orders.

data>labs.note: Web crawls, licensed archives, code and synthetic data are assembled into training corpora.

talent>labs.note: Researchers move between universities, big companies and start-ups; founding teams seed new labs.

labs>models.note: Training runs produce model weights; a few runs per year set the record for compute used.

models>products.note: Models are served through chat apps, coding tools and APIs; serving cost falls as hardware and methods improve.

products>users.note: Products reach the public in months rather than years when distribution is already in place.

users>data.note: Conversations, ratings and corrections become feedback data for the next round of training.

products>capital.note: Subscriptions and API revenue flow back to labs and justify the next round of spending.

policy>labs.note: Safety rules, disclosure duties and liability shape what labs release and how.

policy>chips.note: Export controls decide which countries and companies can buy the most capable accelerators.

policy>data.note: Privacy law and copyright rulings decide what may be collected and trained on.

what: Training and serving models happens in data centers that run around the clock and draw power from the grid.
Because the largest clusters need steady supply for years, developers now sign long-term power contracts, including deals to restart nuclear plants and build new generation.

number.how: Latest IEA estimate at or before the scrubbed year, projections excluded. Estimates from different IEA reports use different scopes.

energy.read: The ticks around the ring are the energy events in the record, colored by domain; the number is the measured electricity use for the year on the scrub.

what: Specialized accelerators, mostly GPUs and a few custom designs, do the arithmetic that training and inference require.
Few firms design them and fewer still can fabricate them at the leading edge, which is why supply, export rules and fab locations matter.
One company's data center sales are the clearest public gauge of this layer's growth.

number.how: NVIDIA Data Center segment revenue, fiscal year matching the scrubbed year's label. Fiscal years end in late January, so FY2026 is mostly calendar 2025.

chips.read: Flows into Chips are power and capital spending; flows out are compute to the labs and the export controls that gate who can buy.

what: Models learn from very large collections of text, images, code and audio, much of it gathered from the open web and from licensed archives.
What may be collected, and whether training on copyrighted work is lawful, is being settled in courts and legislatures.
The count of AI papers is one of the few measures of the field's output that runs back decades.

number.how: arXiv papers listed in cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL or cs.CV, counted by first submission date, for the scrubbed year. The 2026 count is partial.

data.read: Data flows into the labs as corpora and comes back from users as feedback; the Rules layer shows where law cuts across it.

what: A few thousand researchers and engineers carry the methods between universities, large companies and start-ups.
Moves of senior researchers, founding teams and public warnings from pioneers are events in this record; the Lineage strip below tracks who left where to found what.
Worldwide publication counts give a rough measure of how many people are working on the subject.

number.how: Scholarly publications on AI worldwide, latest year at or before the scrubbed year, from CSET's corpus via Our World in Data. Recent years are incomplete.

talent.read: The single flow out of Talent goes to the labs; the lab count in the Labs card is one result of those moves.

what: Venture rounds, strategic investments by cloud providers and chipmakers, and the internal budgets of large companies pay for everything else.
Money enters at two points, as funding to labs and as capital spending on chips and data centers, and comes back as revenue from products.
The private investment series counts funding to AI companies and is reported in constant dollars, so it is lower than nominal headlines.

number.how: Global private investment in AI companies for the scrubbed year, constant 2021 dollars, from the Stanford AI Index via Our World in Data.

capital.read: Follow the Money layer: funding and capex leave this organ, revenue returns to it from Products.

what: Labs combine compute, data, talent and capital into training runs and decide what to release.
They range from research groups inside large companies to start-ups founded by people who left those groups; their governance disputes and partnerships are part of the record.

number.how: Organizations in the Lineage data founded between 2010 and the scrubbed year.

labs.read: Every input layer converges here; the single output is Models. Click a neighbor in the list to follow a flow.

what: Models are the trained weights that turn compute and data into capabilities, released as closed services, gated research weights or open downloads.
Compute behind record training runs, this card's key number, has grown by orders of magnitude; it is the clearest single measure of frontier movement.

number.how: Largest training compute recorded for any model by the scrubbed year, from Epoch AI's notable models dataset. That series also draws this diagram's Labs to Models flow.

models.read: Training flows in from the labs; inference flows out to products. Ticks around the ring are the model events, the densest organ in the record.

what: Chat assistants, coding tools, search features and APIs are how models reach people and earn revenue.
The cost of serving a fixed level of capability has fallen quickly, which is what lets products spread to hundreds of millions of people.
Incidents involving deployed systems, from robotaxis to chatbots, are recorded here too.

number.how: Lowest price per million tokens for a model matching GPT-4 (March 2023) on MMLU, among points up to the scrubbed year, from Epoch AI.

products.read: Inference flows in from Models; access flows out to Users and revenue flows back to Capital.

what: The public adopts, tests, misuses and reacts to the products, and its behavior feeds back as data and as politics.
Time to reach one hundred million people is a common adoption yardstick, though each count uses its own definition.
Public fears and hopes, films, open letters and scandals are recorded as events in this organ.

number.how: Shortest recorded time to a hundred million users among products launched by the scrubbed year; definitions vary by product.

users.read: Access arrives from Products; feedback leaves toward Data.

what: Policy covers laws, executive orders, export controls, court rulings and international declarations that bound the rest of this system.
Rules act at three points, on labs through safety and disclosure duties, on chips through export controls, and on data through privacy and copyright.

number.how: Measures in the Policy atlas enacted, in force or introduced by the scrubbed year.

policy.read: Policy has no inputs in this diagram; its three outputs make up the Rules layer.
